set1.q: A 34-year-old woman is brought in after a car crash with a heart rate of 128 and a blood pressure of 88/56. The rhythm is regular with a normal P wave before every narrow QRS. Bedside ultrasound shows free fluid in the abdomen. Which is the most appropriate approach to her heart rate?
opts: Adenosine is used in stable supraventricular tachycardia after a vagal maneuver, to convert the rhythm or slow it enough to see P waves. Her P waves are already visible before every QRS, and her sinus rate is a response to blood loss. Tell: a normal P wave before each QRS plus an obvious cause means sinus tachycardia, so treat the cause.

Synchronized cardioversion is for hemodynamically unstable tachyarrhythmias such as supraventricular tachycardia, atrial flutter or atrial fibrillation. Her rhythm is sinus, driven by bleeding, so a shock would leave the cause untouched. Tell: a sinus P wave before every QRS rules out cardioversion; appropriate sinus tachycardia is managed by treating the cause.

Within sinus tachycardia, beta blockers come up only for the inappropriate form, a diagnosis of exclusion with no secondary cause, and even there they are not well tolerated. Her tachycardia has an obvious cause, hypovolemia from bleeding, which makes it appropriate. Tell: an identified cause means treat the cause, not the rate.

Correct. A regular rhythm at 128 with a normal P wave before every narrow QRS is sinus tachycardia, and with a blood pressure of 88/56 and free abdominal fluid after a crash it is an appropriate response to hypovolemia. Appropriate sinus tachycardia is managed by treating the underlying cause, here the bleeding.

set1.q: A 28-year-old woman has sudden palpitations after three energy drinks. She notices her neck throbbing, and examination shows a frog sign (rapid visible pulsations in the neck). Her heart rate is 172 and regular, with a narrow QRS and no visible P waves. She has no heart disease. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Multifocal atrial tachycardia is irregular, with at least three P-wave shapes, and occurs in acutely ill patients with severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease or heart failure. She is healthy and her rhythm is regular with no visible P waves. Tell: changing P waves in a sick lung patient is multifocal; hidden P waves after a stimulant is nodal reentry.

Atrial fibrillation is irregularly irregular with absent P waves, often in older patients with hypertension, diabetes or heart disease. Her rhythm is regular, which points to a reentry circuit. Tell: both may show no P waves, but only atrial fibrillation is irregularly irregular.
ruled out by a stated finding

Sinus tachycardia runs at over 100 to 160 with a uniform P wave before every QRS. Her rate is 172 with no visible P waves, a sudden onset and neck pulsations. Tell: a normal P wave before each QRS means sinus; hidden P waves with the frog sign point to nodal reentry.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. A sudden, regular narrow tachycardia at 172 with hidden P waves, neck pulsations (frog sign) and a caffeine trigger in a young woman without heart disease is atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia. It is a reentry circuit within the node, far more common in women, and usually runs at 140 to 180.

set1.q: A 27-year-old woman has had 20 minutes of sudden palpitations. Her heart rate is 188, blood pressure 122/76, and she is alert with no chest pain or breathlessness. The electrocardiogram shows a regular narrow complex tachycardia with no visible P waves. Which is the most appropriate first step?
opts: Intravenous procainamide is used when Wolff-Parkinson-White is known or adenosine reveals atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White; it is not a first step. Her rhythm is regular and narrow with no pre-excitation described. Tell: a stable regular narrow tachycardia starts with a vagal maneuver.

Correct. A sudden, regular narrow complex tachycardia at 188 with no visible P waves is supraventricular tachycardia, and with a blood pressure of 122/76, a clear mind and no chest pain or breathlessness she is stable. A vagal maneuver is first line, followed by adenosine, which may slow the rhythm enough to show P waves.

Adenosine is the second step for stable supraventricular tachycardia, given if a vagal maneuver fails, and it may be repeated once. The question asks for the first step, which needs no drug. Tell: vagal maneuver first, then adenosine.

Immediate synchronized cardioversion is for hemodynamically unstable supraventricular tachycardia. She is alert, with a blood pressure of 122/76 and no chest pain or breathlessness, so she is stable. Tell: a fast rate alone is not instability; look at blood pressure and mental status.

set1.q: A 66-year-old man had coronary bypass surgery two months ago. He now has palpitations and fatigue. His heart rate is 150 and regular, and the electrocardiogram shows sawtooth waves, two for every narrow QRS. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Sinus tachycardia has one uniform P wave before each QRS, at over 100 to 160. He has two sawtooth waves for each QRS, so the atria are beating at twice the ventricular rate. Tell: one P wave per QRS is sinus; two sawtooth waves per QRS is flutter with 2:1 block.
ruled out by a stated finding

Multifocal atrial tachycardia is irregular, with one P wave per QRS in at least three distinct shapes. His rhythm is regular with two matching sawtooth waves per QRS. Tell: changing P shapes, one per beat, mean multiple foci; a regular sawtooth with two waves per beat is flutter.

Correct. A regular rate of 150 with two sawtooth waves for every narrow QRS is atrial flutter with 2:1 block, the most common ratio, in which the node blocks one of every two atrial impulses. Atrial scarring or damage from surgery, such as his recent bypass operation, is a common setting for flutter.

Atrial fibrillation is irregularly irregular with absent P waves and no organized atrial waves. His rhythm is regular at 150 with repeating sawtooth waves. Tell: regular with sawtooth waves is flutter; irregularly irregular without P waves is fibrillation.
ruled out by a stated finding

set1.q: A 77-year-old man had cardiac surgery last year. A rhythm strip shows normal sinus beats, then a sudden pause with no P wave, after which narrow beats at 45 appear with no visible P waves. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Sinus arrhythmia is a normal, physiologic rhythm at 60 to 100 that varies with breathing, with a uniform P wave before every QRS. A sudden pause followed by slow beats with no P waves in a man after cardiac surgery is pathologic. Tell: sinus arrhythmia never loses its P waves or stops abruptly.

Atrial flutter shows sawtooth waves at an atrial rate of 250 or more, outnumbering the QRS complexes. This strip shows a flat pause followed by slow narrow beats with no atrial waves at all. Tell: flutter fills the baseline with waves; sinus arrest leaves it empty and then hands over to a junctional rhythm.

Correct. Normal sinus beats followed by a sudden pause with no P wave mean the sinus node stopped generating impulses: sinus arrest, a form of sick sinus syndrome. The escape rhythm is junctional, narrow beats at 45 with no visible P waves. Injury to the sinus node from cardiac surgery is a listed cause, matching his history.

Sinus bradycardia is a regular rhythm under 60 with a uniform P wave before every QRS. This strip shows a sudden pause and then narrow beats with no P waves, so the sinus node is not driving the slow beats at all. Tell: in sinus bradycardia every beat still has its P wave.

set1.q: A 59-year-old man has frequent premature atrial contractions on a monitor (early beats with abnormal P waves), many per minute. He has no known heart disease. Which evaluation is most appropriate?
opts: No treatment is needed when premature atrial contractions are infrequent and asymptomatic. His are frequent, many per minute, and frequent beats call for a search for underlying structural heart disease. Tell: frequency is the switch; infrequent means reassure, frequent means evaluate.

Correct. His premature atrial contractions are frequent, many per minute, and when they are frequent the step is to look for underlying structural heart disease. In patients with heart disease these beats may precede paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia, atrial fibrillation or atrial flutter, which makes the search worthwhile.

Testing for an accessory pathway fits a short PR interval with a delta wave on the resting tracing, the pattern of Wolff-Parkinson-White. His finding is frequent early beats with abnormal P waves, which are premature atrial contractions. Tell: frequent premature atrial contractions prompt a structural heart workup, not a pathway search.

A digoxin level matters when digoxin toxicity is suspected, which is a listed cause of junctional rhythm, not of premature atrial contractions. He has frequent early beats with abnormal P waves and no stated digoxin use. Tell: frequent premature atrial beats send you looking for structural heart disease.

set1.q: A 61-year-old man's frequent premature atrial contractions are shown on monitoring to trigger his episodes of atrial fibrillation. Referral for which procedure is most appropriate?
opts: Septal myectomy is not a treatment for premature atrial contractions. When these beats are frequent or are shown to trigger atrial fibrillation, as on his monitor, catheter ablation is the procedure used. Tell: the procedure has to target the early atrial beats themselves, which ablation does.

Correct. His premature atrial contractions are frequent and monitoring shows them triggering atrial fibrillation, the two settings in which catheter ablation is used. Otherwise, persistent symptomatic premature atrial contractions are treated with a beta blocker such as metoprolol if not contraindicated.

A permanent pacemaker treats chronic symptomatic bradycardia, such as sick sinus syndrome with symptomatic slow rates. His problem is early atrial beats that set off atrial fibrillation, not a slow rate. Tell: premature atrial beats that trigger fibrillation are targeted by catheter ablation.

Carotid endarterectomy is not a treatment for premature atrial contractions, which arise in the atria. When they are frequent or trigger atrial fibrillation, catheter ablation is the listed procedure. Tell: an arrhythmia trigger is treated at its source in the heart, by ablation.

set1.q: A 42-year-old man has paroxysmal atrial fibrillation and no hypertension, diabetes, heart failure, stroke or vascular disease, so his CHA2DS2-VASc (stroke risk) score is 0. Which anticoagulation plan is most appropriate?
opts: Direct oral anticoagulants are the preferred agents in nonvalvular atrial fibrillation when anticoagulation is needed. With a CHA2DS2-VASc (stroke-risk) score of 0 in a man, he is low risk and may not require anticoagulation at all. Tell: the score decides whether to anticoagulate before the choice of drug matters.

A home heparin infusion is not a listed option; the anticoagulants listed for atrial fibrillation are direct oral anticoagulants or warfarin. With a CHA2DS2-VASc (stroke-risk) score of 0 in a man, anticoagulation may not be needed. Tell: low score, possibly no anticoagulant.

Correct. His CHA2DS2-VASc (stroke-risk) score is 0: age under 65 (0), male (0), and no heart failure, hypertension, stroke, vascular disease or diabetes. A score of 0 in a man, or 1 in a woman, is low risk and may not require anticoagulation.

Warfarin with a target international normalized ratio (INR) of 2 to 3 is used when anticoagulation is needed and a direct oral anticoagulant is not chosen. His CHA2DS2-VASc (stroke-risk) score of 0 is low risk and may not require anticoagulation. Tell: decide on the need first; 0 in a man is low risk.

set1.q: A 19-year-old woman with Wolff-Parkinson-White has had three emergency visits for reentrant tachycardia this year. Which long-term management is first line?
opts: Adenosine is an acute drug, first line for orthodromic reentry, and it must never be used if atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White appears. It is not a long-term therapy. Tell: chronic management of Wolff-Parkinson-White is catheter ablation of the pathway.

A permanent pacemaker treats chronic symptomatic bradycardia, such as sick sinus syndrome. Her problem is recurrent fast reentry through an accessory pathway. Tell: pacemakers support slow rhythms; ablation removes a pathway.

Anticoagulation is part of managing atrial fibrillation and atrial flutter, guided by stroke risk. It does not treat an accessory pathway or prevent reentrant tachycardia. Tell: the long-term fix for Wolff-Parkinson-White is ablating the pathway.

Correct. She has Wolff-Parkinson-White with recurrent reentrant tachycardia, and for chronic management of Wolff-Parkinson-White, catheter ablation of the accessory pathway is the first-line treatment. Acute episodes otherwise rely on adenosine, which must never be used if atrial fibrillation with the pathway appears.

set1.q: A 79-year-old woman has had atrial fibrillation for years and asks why her clinician insists on a blood thinner. Which complication is the anticoagulant meant to prevent?
opts: Correct. Anticoagulation in atrial fibrillation is about stroke risk, assessed with the CHA2DS2-VASc (stroke-risk) score, and patients typically require it unless bleeding risk is high. At 79 she scores 2 points for age 75 or older and 1 for female sex, so a blood thinner is expected.

Anticoagulants are not used to prevent heart block; in atrial fibrillation their purpose is lowering stroke risk, measured with the CHA2DS2-VASc (stroke-risk) score. Tell: a blood thinner in atrial fibrillation targets clots and stroke, not conduction.

Anticoagulants are not used to prevent ventricular fibrillation; in atrial fibrillation they are given according to stroke risk, measured with the CHA2DS2-VASc (stroke-risk) score. Tell: the anticoagulant decision rests on a stroke-risk score, so its target is stroke.

Rate control drugs, given intravenously or by mouth, manage the heart rate in atrial fibrillation. Anticoagulants are a separate part of management aimed at stroke risk. Tell: rate control handles the rate; the blood thinner handles stroke risk.

set1.q: A 71-year-old man with a slow sinus rhythm at 34 is hypotensive and drowsy. Two doses of atropine have not changed his rate or blood pressure. Which is the next step?
opts: Correct. A sinus rhythm at 34 with hypotension and drowsiness is acute, symptomatic, hemodynamically unstable bradycardia, and atropine, the first-line drug, has failed after two doses. The next step is a temporary pacemaker; a permanent pacemaker is for chronic symptomatic bradycardia.

Adenosine is used in stable supraventricular tachycardia after a vagal maneuver, to convert the rhythm or slow it enough to reveal P waves. Slowing a heart already at 34 is the opposite of the goal. Tell: after failed atropine in unstable bradycardia, use a temporary pacemaker.

Synchronized cardioversion, a timed shock at decreased voltage, treats unstable tachycardias such as supraventricular tachycardia or atrial fibrillation. His rhythm is slow at 34, the opposite problem. Tell: unstable and slow after atropine means a temporary pacemaker.

Metoprolol is a beta blocker, and beta blockers are a listed cause of sinus bradycardia, so it would slow him further. Tell: a drug that causes bradycardia is never the rescue; the sequence for unstable bradycardia is atropine, then a temporary pacemaker.

set1.q: A 24-year-old man is told his electrocardiogram shows a normal P wave before each narrow QRS at 68 beats per minute, with the rate rising as he breathes in and falling as he breathes out. He worries that he has heart disease. Which counseling is most accurate?
opts: Anticoagulation is part of managing atrial fibrillation and atrial flutter, guided by stroke risk. Sinus arrhythmia is a normal, physiologic rhythm with a P wave before every beat. Tell: a normal sinus P wave before each QRS means no atrial fibrillation and no anticoagulation question.

Correct. A normal P wave before each narrow QRS at 68, with the rate rising on inspiration and falling on expiration, is sinus arrhythmia. It is a normal, physiologic rhythm, irregular with a pattern at 60 to 100, so he can be reassured that it is not heart disease and needs no treatment.

A permanent pacemaker is for chronic symptomatic bradycardia or sick sinus syndrome with correlated symptoms. His rate is 68 with a breathing-linked variation and normal P waves, a normal finding. Tell: a patterned variation at 60 to 100 is physiologic, not a pacemaker problem.

Stopping exercise has no basis here; sinus arrhythmia is a normal, physiologic rhythm tied to breathing. Tell: the rate rising on inspiration and falling on expiration is expected, so reassurance, not restriction, is the counseling for this healthy young man.

set1.q: An 81-year-old man has known tachy-brady syndrome (a fast rhythm alternating with slow rates and pauses) and asks which fast rhythm is behind his palpitations. An ambulatory monitor is arranged. Which rhythm is it most likely to record during the fast episodes?
opts: Ventricular tachycardia can be the fast rhythm in some patients with tachy-brady syndrome, who then need a permanent pacemaker with an implantable defibrillator. It is not the most common one; atrial fibrillation is. Tell: ventricular tachycardia changes the device, not the most likely rhythm.

A junctional rhythm is a slow, regular rhythm usually at 40 to 60 with inverted or hidden P waves, and it can follow sinus arrest. It could appear in his slow phases, not his fast ones. Tell: junctional rhythm belongs to the brady side; atrial fibrillation is the usual tachy side.

Correct. In tachy-brady syndrome, the form of sick sinus syndrome in which a fast rhythm alternates with slow rates or pauses, the tachyarrhythmia is most commonly atrial fibrillation. During his fast episodes the monitor would most likely show an irregularly irregular rhythm without P waves.

Atrial flutter is an organized atrial rhythm with sawtooth waves at an atrial rate of 250 or more, but it is not the named most-common fast rhythm of tachy-brady syndrome. That is atrial fibrillation. Tell: in tachy-brady syndrome, expect an irregularly irregular fast phase, not a regular sawtooth.

set1.q: A 70-year-old woman with right-sided heart failure has atrial flutter (sawtooth flutter waves) with a ventricular rate of 140. She is alert, with a blood pressure of 124/78 and no chest pain. Which is the most appropriate initial treatment?
opts: Synchronized cardioversion is for hemodynamically unstable atrial flutter, and an elective outpatient cardioversion comes only after 21 days of anticoagulation. She is alert with a normal blood pressure and no chest pain. Tell: stable flutter starts with rate control; instability is what earns the shock.

Adenosine, repeated once if needed, is the second step for stable supraventricular tachycardia after a vagal maneuver; it is not the listed treatment for atrial flutter. Stable flutter is rate controlled with a beta blocker or calcium channel blocker. Tell: once sawtooth waves are visible, the diagnosis is made and rate control follows.

A permanent pacemaker treats chronic symptomatic bradycardia, a slow rate. Her flutter has a ventricular rate of 140, which needs slowing with a beta blocker or calcium channel blocker. Tell: a pacemaker does not treat a fast atrial rhythm; ablation is the definitive step for flutter.
A beta or calcium channel blocker

Correct. Sawtooth flutter waves with a ventricular rate of 140 in a woman with right-sided heart failure are atrial flutter, and she is alert with a blood pressure of 124/78 and no chest pain, so she is stable. Stable flutter is rate controlled with a beta blocker or calcium channel blocker, though control is harder to achieve than in atrial fibrillation.

set1.q: A 64-year-old man is admitted with an inferior myocardial infarction. His heart rate falls to 46 with narrow QRS complexes and P waves that are either inverted (retrograde P waves) or buried in the QRS. Which rhythm is most likely?
opts: Correct. A regular, narrow-complex rhythm at 46 with P waves inverted or buried in the QRS means the impulse starts in the atrioventricular (AV) node: a junctional rhythm, usually 40 to 60. When the low node fires first the P wave is retrograde, after the QRS; mid-node firing buries it. Inferior myocardial infarction is a listed cause.

Sinus bradycardia fits the slow rate, but the impulse starts in the sinus node, so every QRS has a uniform P wave before it with a PR of 0.12 to 0.20 seconds. P waves that are inverted after the QRS or buried in it do not fit. Tell: same slow rate, but a junctional rhythm loses the normal P wave and PR interval.
ruled out by a stated finding

Atrial flutter fills the baseline with sawtooth flutter waves at an atrial rate of 250 or more, outnumbering the QRS complexes. This man has a slow rate of 46 and only one P wave per beat, inverted or buried in the QRS. Tell: sawtooth waves mean flutter; a single retrograde or hidden P wave means a junctional origin.

Focal atrial tachycardia is a fast rhythm, over 100 and usually 150 to 250, from one ectopic atrial focus, with one consistently abnormal P wave before each QRS and a normal PR of 0.12 to 0.20 seconds. His rate is 46 and his P waves are inverted or buried. Tell: fast with a P before every QRS is atrial; slow with retrograde P waves is junctional.
ruled out by a stated finding

set1.q: A 75-year-old man has a junctional rhythm at 42 with dizziness. Monitoring shows that the cause is high-grade atrioventricular block. Which treatment is indicated?
opts: Correct. A junctional rhythm at 42 with dizziness, caused by high-grade atrioventricular block, needs a permanent pacemaker. Management of junctional rhythm depends on the cause, and complete or high-grade block or sick sinus syndrome is the setting for a pacemaker.

No treatment suits a junctional rhythm in an asymptomatic, otherwise healthy person, such as an athlete with high vagal tone. He is dizzy and has high-grade atrioventricular block behind it. Tell: block as the cause means a permanent pacemaker, not observation.

Adenosine is used in stable supraventricular tachycardia to convert the rhythm or slow it enough to reveal P waves. His rhythm is already slow at 42 from high-grade block, so slowing it further is the opposite of the goal. Tell: block plus a slow junctional rhythm calls for a pacemaker.

Catheter ablation is used for tachycardias, such as focal atrial tachycardia, nodal reentry or an accessory pathway. A slow junctional rhythm from high-grade block needs a permanent pacemaker. Tell: ablation removes fast circuits; it does not fix block.

set1.q: A 68-year-old man is brought in confused, with a blood pressure of 76/40. The monitor shows a slow, regular rhythm at 36 with a normal P wave before every narrow QRS. Which is the first-line treatment?
opts: A permanent pacemaker is for chronic, symptomatic bradycardia, not the first step in an acute, unstable episode. The acute sequence is atropine, then a temporary pacemaker if atropine fails. Tell: acute and unstable means atropine first; a permanent device comes later if the problem is chronic.

Correct. A slow, regular rhythm at 36 with a normal P wave before every narrow QRS is sinus bradycardia, and confusion with a blood pressure of 76/40 make it acute, symptomatic and hemodynamically unstable. Atropine is first line; if it fails, a temporary pacemaker follows.

Adenosine is used in stable supraventricular tachycardia after a vagal maneuver, to convert the rhythm or slow it enough to reveal P waves. Slowing a rhythm already at 36 in a confused, hypotensive man is the opposite of the goal. Tell: adenosine is for fast narrow rhythms; atropine is for unstable slow ones.

Synchronized cardioversion, a timed shock at decreased voltage, treats hemodynamically unstable tachycardias such as supraventricular tachycardia or atrial fibrillation. His rhythm is slow at 36, the opposite problem. Tell: unstable and fast means a synchronized shock; unstable and slow means atropine.

set1.q: A 58-year-old woman has new fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance and constipation. Her pulse is 50 and regular, with a normal P wave before each narrow QRS. She takes no medications. Which test is most useful next?
opts: Correct. A regular rate of 50 with a normal P wave before each narrow QRS is sinus bradycardia, and with no medications the drug causes are excluded. Hypothyroidism is a listed cause, and her fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance and constipation point to it, so thyroid testing comes next.

Digoxin is a listed drug cause of sinus bradycardia, but she takes no medications, so a level would not help. Her fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance and constipation point instead to hypothyroidism, another listed cause. Tell: no drug exposure rules out the drug causes.
ruled out by a stated finding

An electrophysiology study is not among the listed steps for sinus bradycardia. Her symptoms point to a listed, treatable cause, hypothyroidism, which is checked with thyroid tests. Tell: look for the underlying cause first when the history already suggests one.

Ambulatory monitoring is used in suspected sick sinus syndrome to see whether symptoms correlate with episodes of bradycardia. Her rhythm is a steady sinus bradycardia, and her symptoms suggest hypothyroidism, a listed cause checked with thyroid tests. Tell: weight gain and cold intolerance point to the thyroid, not to pauses.

Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
set1.q: A 38-year-old woman notices occasional skipped beats during a stressful month of heavy coffee and wine. Her electrocardiogram shows occasional early beats with an abnormally shaped P wave and a narrow QRS, and her examination and echocardiogram are normal. Which advice is most appropriate?
opts: A beta blocker such as metoprolol is for premature atrial contractions that are persistent and symptomatic, if not contraindicated. Hers are occasional and tied to coffee, wine and stress that she can cut back. Tell: start with avoiding triggers and reassurance; a beta blocker is held for persistent symptoms.

Catheter ablation is used when premature atrial contractions are frequent or are triggering atrial fibrillation. Hers are occasional, her heart is normal on examination and echocardiogram, and clear triggers are present. Tell: occasional beats with obvious triggers get counseling and reassurance, not a procedure.

Anticoagulation is part of managing atrial fibrillation and atrial flutter, guided by stroke risk. She has isolated premature atrial contractions in a normal heart, which carry no such indication. Tell: early beats with a P wave are not fibrillation, and they need counseling rather than anticoagulation.

Correct. Occasional early beats with an abnormal P wave and a narrow QRS are premature atrial contractions, and in a normal heart they occur with excess alcohol, stress and caffeine, all present in her month. Management is to counsel avoidance of these precipitants and reassure her about the benign nature of the rhythm.

set1.io: Identify medical care strategies for atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias for the following populations. 3. adult 4. elderly
set1.q: A 76-year-old woman with hypertension and diabetes has nonvalvular atrial fibrillation and a high CHA2DS2-VASc (stroke risk) score. Which anticoagulant class is preferred?
opts: Aspirin is not among the anticoagulants listed for atrial fibrillation, and it appears on the HAS-BLED (bleeding-risk) score as a medication that predisposes to bleeding. Her high stroke-risk score calls for anticoagulation, preferably a direct oral anticoagulant. Tell: aspirin adds bleeding risk without being the recommended stroke protection.

Her age adds to stroke risk rather than ruling out anticoagulation: 75 or older scores 2 points on the stroke-risk score. With a high score, patients typically require anticoagulation unless bleeding risk is high, a HAS-BLED (bleeding-risk) score of 3 or more. Tell: only a high bleeding score withholds anticoagulation, not age itself.

Correct. Her CHA2DS2-VASc (stroke-risk) score is high (age 75 or older 2, female 1, hypertension 1, diabetes 1 = 5), so she typically requires anticoagulation unless bleeding risk is high. In nonvalvular atrial fibrillation the direct oral anticoagulants (dabigatran, apixaban, edoxaban or rivaroxaban) are preferred.

Warfarin can be used, with a target international normalized ratio (INR) of 2 to 3, but it is not the preferred class. In nonvalvular atrial fibrillation the direct oral anticoagulants are preferred. Tell: preferred means a direct oral anticoagulant; warfarin is the alternative with its own target range.

Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
set1.q: A 44-year-old man has focal atrial tachycardia at 165. He is hemodynamically stable but symptomatic with palpitations. Which acute treatment is appropriate?
opts: An unsynchronized shock is not a listed treatment for focal atrial tachycardia; synchronized cardioversion is used only if the patient is unstable. He is stable, so he gets an intravenous beta blocker or nondihydropyridine calcium channel blocker. Tell: stable and symptomatic means intravenous rate control.

Intravenous magnesium is not among the listed acute treatments for focal atrial tachycardia. A hemodynamically stable, symptomatic patient like him gets an intravenous beta blocker or nondihydropyridine calcium channel blocker while the cause is sought. Tell: stable focal atrial tachycardia is rate controlled intravenously.

Correct. He has focal atrial tachycardia at 165, hemodynamically stable but symptomatic with palpitations. That is treated with an intravenous beta blocker or nondihydropyridine calcium channel blocker while the underlying cause and precipitating factors are identified and treated.

Atropine is first line for acute, symptomatic, unstable bradycardia, a slow rhythm. His focal atrial tachycardia is fast at 165, so raising the rate is the opposite of the goal. Tell: atropine is for slow rhythms; stable focal atrial tachycardia gets an intravenous beta blocker.

Atrioventricular block b. Bundle branch blocks c. Ventricular premature beats d. Ventricular tachycardia e. Ventricular fibrillation f. Torsades de Pointes g. Idioventricular rhythm h. Junctional rhythm i. QT prolongation
set1.q: A 57-year-old woman has frequent premature junctional contractions, more than 10 per minute, on a monitor. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: A permanent pacemaker is for slow rhythms, such as a junctional rhythm caused by complete or high-grade block or sick sinus syndrome. She has frequent early beats, not a slow escape rhythm. Tell: frequent premature beats call for a structural workup and a beta blocker, not a device.

Anticoagulation is part of managing atrial fibrillation and atrial flutter, guided by stroke risk. Premature junctional contractions are early beats from the atrioventricular junction, and frequent ones prompt a search for structural heart disease instead. Tell: frequent junctional beats lead to a structural workup, not anticoagulation.

Correct. Premature junctional contractions that are frequent, more than 10 per minute or multifocal, prompt a search for underlying structural heart disease, and the beats are then treated with a beta blocker. Her rate of more than 10 per minute meets that threshold.

Reassurance alone suits premature junctional contractions that are asymptomatic and infrequent. Hers are more than 10 per minute, the frequency threshold that prompts a search for structural heart disease. Tell: more than 10 per minute or multifocal means evaluate and treat.

Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
set1.q: A 79-year-old man has tachy-brady syndrome (a fast rhythm alternating with slow rates and pauses) on monitoring, and he faints during the pauses. Thyroid tests and electrolytes are normal and he takes no rate-slowing drugs. Which treatment is most appropriate?
opts: Atropine is first line for acute, symptomatic, hemodynamically unstable bradycardia, a short-term rescue. His fainting comes from recurrent pauses that correlate with his symptoms, which calls for a permanent pacemaker. Tell: recurrent symptomatic pauses need a device, not an as-needed drug.

Ablation alone does not address the pauses that make him faint. When symptoms correlate with bradycardia in sick sinus syndrome, a permanent pacemaker is placed, and tachy-brady syndrome often needs one. Tell: fainting during pauses means pacing.

Observation is appropriate in sick sinus syndrome only when symptoms do not correlate with episodes of bradycardia. He faints during the pauses, so they clearly correlate. Tell: correlated symptoms move management to a permanent pacemaker.

Correct. He faints during the pauses of tachy-brady syndrome, so his symptoms correlate with the bradycardia, and the reversible causes (thyroid disease, electrolyte abnormalities, rate-slowing drugs) have been excluded. Symptomatic bradycardia in sick sinus syndrome is treated with a permanent pacemaker, and tachy-brady syndrome often needs one.

Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
set1.q: A 72-year-old man with hypertension, diabetes and obstructive sleep apnea has had palpitations for two days. His pulse is irregularly irregular at 132, and the electrocardiogram shows no P waves and a narrow QRS. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Multifocal atrial tachycardia is irregular but keeps a P wave before every QRS, in at least three shapes, usually in acutely ill patients with lung disease or heart failure. His tracing has no P waves. Tell: no P waves in an irregular narrow rhythm means fibrillation.
ruled out by a stated finding

Atrial flutter with a fixed 2:1 block is regular, with two sawtooth flutter waves per QRS. His rhythm is irregularly irregular with no atrial waves. Tell: regular with sawtooth waves is flutter; irregularly irregular without P waves is fibrillation.
ruled out by a stated finding

Sinus arrhythmia keeps a uniform P wave before every beat at 60 to 100, with a rate that follows breathing. He has no P waves and a rate of 132. Tell: sinus arrhythmia is patterned and has P waves; atrial fibrillation has neither.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. An irregularly irregular, narrow-complex rhythm at 132 with no P waves is atrial fibrillation, within its usual 110 to 160. Hypertension, diabetes, sleep apnea and older age, all present in this man, are among the conditions in which it is commonly seen.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
set1.q: A 24-year-old man whose Wolff-Parkinson-White was found on a school electrocardiogram presents with palpitations. The rhythm is irregular and wide-complex, at rates up to 260, with varying delta waves (slurred upstrokes). He is alert with a blood pressure of 118/74. Which drug is the most appropriate treatment?
opts: Adenosine must never be used when Wolff-Parkinson-White is known or atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White is present; it is first line only for ordinary orthodromic reentry. His irregular, wide, delta-wave complexes in known Wolff-Parkinson-White are exactly that exception. Tell: an irregular wide rhythm with delta waves rules adenosine out.

Intravenous magnesium is not the listed treatment for atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White. Irregular, wide complexes with varying delta waves in a patient with a known accessory pathway call for intravenous procainamide. Tell: known Wolff-Parkinson-White plus a fast irregular rhythm means procainamide.

Atropine is the first-line drug for acute, symptomatic, unstable bradycardia. This man has a very fast, irregular rhythm conducting with Wolff-Parkinson-White, the opposite problem, so atropine has no role. Tell: atropine is for slow rates; known Wolff-Parkinson-White with a fast rhythm calls for procainamide.

Correct. An irregular, wide-complex tachycardia up to 260 with varying delta waves in a man with known Wolff-Parkinson-White is atrial fibrillation conducting over the accessory pathway. When Wolff-Parkinson-White is known, intravenous procainamide is used, never adenosine; he is alert with a normal blood pressure, so a drug is appropriate.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
set1.q: A 70-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation at 150 has crackles throughout both lungs from pulmonary edema and a blood pressure of 82/50. Which feature makes this presentation a medical emergency?
opts: Correct. Crackles throughout both lungs from pulmonary edema and a blood pressure of 82/50 are severe heart failure, one of the listed medical emergencies in atrial fibrillation, along with atrial fibrillation during an acute myocardial infarction. Atrial fibrillation itself is usually not directly life-threatening.

A fast rate, here 150, is rapid ventricular response, which in a stable patient is treated with intravenous rate control. A fast rate is not by itself one of the listed emergencies; severe heart failure is. Tell: the emergency is defined by heart failure or acute infarction, not by the rate alone.

An irregularly irregular pulse simply defines atrial fibrillation, which is usually not directly life-threatening. The emergency here comes from severe heart failure with pulmonary edema and hypotension. Tell: the rhythm's irregularity is the diagnosis, not the danger.

Older age is a listed risk for developing atrial fibrillation and raises the stroke-risk score, but it does not make a presentation an emergency. Severe heart failure, with pulmonary edema and hypotension, does. Tell: age raises risk over time; heart failure makes it urgent now.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
set1.q: A 38-year-old woman has recurrent, symptomatic focal atrial tachycardia despite an oral beta blocker. She wants a definitive option. Referral for which procedure is most appropriate?
opts: Anticoagulation is part of managing atrial fibrillation and atrial flutter, guided by stroke risk. It does not treat a focal atrial tachycardia, which comes from a single ectopic focus. Tell: the definitive option for an ectopic focus is catheter ablation.

Correct. Her focal atrial tachycardia keeps recurring despite an oral beta blocker, the initial chronic therapy, and she wants a definitive option. Catheter ablation is usually curative for focal atrial tachycardia, in about 90 percent.

A permanent pacemaker treats chronic symptomatic bradycardia, such as sick sinus syndrome. Focal atrial tachycardia is a fast rhythm from an ectopic atrial focus, which catheter ablation usually cures. Tell: pacemakers support slow rhythms; ablation removes a fast focus.

Adenosine is usually less effective at terminating focal atrial tachycardia than node-dependent reentry, which is why it serves as a diagnostic tool. It is not a definitive or long-term option. Tell: adenosine helps diagnose focal atrial tachycardia; ablation cures it.

Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
set1.q: A 54-year-old man has a regular narrow complex tachycardia at 210. His blood pressure is 72/40, and he is confused and sweating. Which is the most appropriate immediate treatment?
opts: Correct. A regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 210 with a blood pressure of 72/40, confusion and sweating is hemodynamically unstable supraventricular tachycardia, which gets immediate synchronized cardioversion: a timed shock at decreased voltage. Collapse like this is expected once the rate goes above 200, as his has.

A vagal maneuver is the first-line step only for stable supraventricular tachycardia. With a blood pressure of 72/40, sweating and new confusion he is hemodynamically unstable, and immediate synchronized cardioversion comes first. Tell: check blood pressure and mental status before choosing a maneuver over a shock.

Adenosine, repeated once if needed, follows a vagal maneuver in stable supraventricular tachycardia; it may convert the rhythm or slow it enough to show P waves. His blood pressure of 72/40 and confusion make him unstable, so a drug trial would delay the shock he needs. Tell: stable gets vagal maneuver then adenosine; unstable gets cardioversion.

An unsynchronized shock is not the treatment for unstable supraventricular tachycardia; the shock used is synchronized, meaning timed, and given at decreased voltage. He has a pulse and a regular narrow rhythm, the setting for synchronized cardioversion. Tell: an organized narrow-complex rhythm in an unstable patient means a timed, synchronized shock.

Atrioventricular block b. Bundle branch blocks c. Ventricular premature beats d. Ventricular tachycardia e. Ventricular fibrillation f. Torsades de Pointes g. Idioventricular rhythm h. Junctional rhythm i. QT prolongation
set1.q: An 82-year-old woman taking digoxin for heart failure has nausea and fatigue. Her heart rate is 48 and regular, with narrow QRS complexes and retrograde P waves (inverted) just after each QRS in II, III and aVF. Which is the most likely cause of this rhythm?
opts: Correct. A slow, regular, narrow rhythm at 48 with inverted P waves just after each QRS in II, III and aVF is a junctional rhythm, and digoxin toxicity is a listed cause. Her nausea and fatigue while taking digoxin point to toxicity, which is treated with atropine and/or digoxin immune Fab (fragment antigen-binding).

Hyperthyroidism is a listed cause of sinus tachycardia, a fast rhythm with a P wave before each QRS. Her rhythm is slow at 48 with retrograde P waves after the QRS, a junctional rhythm. Tell: a slow junctional rhythm in a patient on digoxin points to digoxin toxicity, not the thyroid.

An accessory pathway (bundle of Kent) shows as pre-excitation, a short PR with a delta wave, and allows fast reentrant tachycardia. Her rhythm is slow and regular at 48 with retrograde P waves, a junctional rhythm. Tell: an accessory pathway goes with fast rhythms and delta waves, not a slow junctional rhythm.

Digoxin toxicity, not missed doses, is the listed digoxin-related cause of junctional rhythm, and digoxin is also a listed cause of sinus bradycardia. A slow junctional rhythm with nausea and fatigue in a patient on digoxin points to too much drug, not too little. Tell: digoxin excess slows the heart; missing doses would not.

Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
set1.q: A 32-year-old woman with recurrent atrioventricular nodal reentry has been taught to stop episodes at home with a vagal maneuver. Tonight an episode stopped within minutes after she did so, and she now feels well. What is the most appropriate advice?
opts: A permanent pacemaker treats chronic symptomatic bradycardia, such as sick sinus syndrome. Nodal reentry is a tachycardia, and an episode she has already ended at home needs no device. Tell: her longer-term options are a pill in the pocket or catheter ablation, not a pacemaker.
No urgent care is usually needed

Correct. She has been educated in vagal maneuvers, her episode of nodal reentry stopped within minutes after one, and she now feels well. When a vagal maneuver terminates nodal reentry at home in an educated patient, urgent medical attention is usually not required, since episodes are usually well tolerated.

An emergency visit is usually not required when an educated patient's vagal maneuver terminates nodal reentry at home and she feels well. Episodes are usually well tolerated, and synchronized cardioversion is rarely needed. Tell: a terminated episode in a well patient can be handled without urgent care.

Anticoagulation is part of managing atrial fibrillation and atrial flutter. Nodal reentry is a regular reentry circuit within the node and is not managed with anticoagulation. Tell: her options are vagal maneuvers, a pill in the pocket or ablation.

Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
set2.q: A 76-year-old woman has episodes of lightheadedness and one faint. A 24-hour ambulatory monitor shows runs of a fast, irregular rhythm that alternate with slow rates and long pauses. Which fast rhythm is most likely on her monitor?
opts: Correct. Runs of a fast, irregular rhythm alternating with slow rates and long pauses, with lightheadedness and a faint, are tachy-brady syndrome, a form of sick sinus syndrome. The tachyarrhythmia in tachy-brady syndrome is most commonly atrial fibrillation, which fits an irregular fast run.

Ventricular fibrillation is not the listed fast rhythm of tachy-brady syndrome, and she has recurring runs she lives through between slow spells. The tachyarrhythmia there is most commonly atrial fibrillation; ventricular tachycardia occurs in some patients and calls for a pacemaker with a defibrillator. Tell: recurring irregular fast runs with pauses are atrial fibrillation.

Sinus tachycardia is regular with a uniform P wave before every QRS. Her fast runs are irregular, and in tachy-brady syndrome the fast rhythm is most commonly atrial fibrillation. Tell: an irregular fast phase alternating with pauses is not sinus; it is atrial fibrillation until proven otherwise.

Nodal reentrant tachycardia is a regular narrow tachycardia, usually 140 to 180, typically in women without heart disease. Her fast runs are irregular and alternate with slow rates and pauses, the pattern of tachy-brady syndrome. Tell: irregular fast runs plus pauses in an older patient point to atrial fibrillation.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
set2.q: A 58-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation started an antiarrhythmic and then develops atrial flutter. Suddenly her ventricular rate matches her atrial rate at 280, with hypotension. Which complication is she now at high risk of?
opts: Multifocal atrial tachycardia is an irregular atrial rhythm with at least three P-wave shapes, seen in acutely ill patients with severe lung disease or heart failure. It is not the danger of 1:1 flutter. Tell: the named risk when every flutter wave conducts is ventricular fibrillation.

Correct. An antiarrhythmic taken for atrial fibrillation is a setting for flutter, and a ventricular rate that now matches the atrial rate at 280 means 1:1 atrial flutter. 1:1 flutter causes extreme hemodynamic instability, as her hypotension shows, and carries a big risk of progression to ventricular fibrillation.

With 1:1 conduction every flutter wave reaches the ventricles, so the ventricular rate equals the atrial rate of 280, not a slow one. That extreme rate causes hemodynamic instability and a big risk of ventricular fibrillation. Tell: 1:1 means the ventricles go as fast as the atria.

Sinus arrest is a form of sick sinus syndrome in which the sinus node does not generate an impulse, leading to a junctional rhythm. It is not the complication of 1:1 atrial flutter. Tell: 1:1 flutter threatens ventricular fibrillation, not a pause.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
set2.q: A 63-year-old man with persistent atrial fibrillation, now rate controlled, wants to try to restore normal rhythm as an outpatient. Which is required before elective cardioversion?
opts: Correct. His persistent atrial fibrillation, continuous for over 7 days but under a year, is stable and rate controlled, and outpatient cardioversion of atrial fibrillation is done after 21 days of anticoagulation. Anticoagulation is part of management for all patients with atrial fibrillation.

A permanent pacemaker treats chronic symptomatic bradycardia, such as sick sinus syndrome, and is not a prerequisite for cardioversion. His rate is controlled, and the requirement before elective cardioversion is 21 days of anticoagulation. Tell: pacemakers answer slow rhythms; elective cardioversion needs anticoagulation.

Rate control is the listed management for stable atrial fibrillation, and stopping it is not the prerequisite for cardioversion. The requirement before elective outpatient cardioversion is 21 days of anticoagulation. Tell: the prerequisite is about clot risk, not the rate.

Adenosine is a step in stable supraventricular tachycardia after a vagal maneuver, to convert a regular narrow rhythm or slow it enough to reveal P waves. It does not prepare a patient for cardioversion of atrial fibrillation. Tell: before elective cardioversion, anticoagulate for 21 days.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
set2.q: A 67-year-old man has had three recurrences of atrial flutter, and rate control has been hard to achieve. Referral for which procedure is most appropriate?
opts: A permanent pacemaker treats chronic symptomatic bradycardia, a slow rhythm. His problem is recurrent flutter with hard-to-control fast rates, which ablation treats definitively. Tell: a pacemaker does not stop a fast atrial rhythm from recurring.

Septal myectomy is not a treatment for atrial flutter. Recurrent flutter that is hard to rate control is referred for ablation, the definitive management of flutter. Tell: the procedure must target the flutter itself, which ablation does.

Carotid endarterectomy is not a treatment for atrial flutter. Recurrent flutter with difficult rate control is referred for ablation, the definitive management, with anticoagulation as part of care. Tell: the heart rhythm is treated in the heart, by ablation.

Correct. Atrial flutter has a substantial recurrence rate and is harder to rate control than atrial fibrillation, both true of his three recurrences and difficult rate control. Ablation is the definitive management of flutter, so referral for catheter ablation fits.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
set2.q: A 19-year-old swimmer has an electrocardiogram before a sports physical. She has no symptoms. The rate is 72, with a normal P wave before every narrow QRS, but the beats come closer together as she breathes in and spread apart as she breathes out. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Correct. A rate of 72 with a normal P wave before every narrow QRS, beats closer together on inspiration and farther apart on expiration, is sinus arrhythmia. It is a normal, physiologic rhythm at 60 to 100 that is irregular with a pattern, which fits a healthy swimmer with no symptoms.

Sick sinus syndrome is an irregular rhythm with variable P waves, from sinus exit block, sinus arrest or tachy-brady swings with pauses. She has a uniform P wave before every beat and a variation tied to breathing, with no pauses. Tell: a breathing-linked pattern is physiologic; pauses and fast-slow swings suggest a diseased node.

Multifocal atrial tachycardia is a fast rhythm, over 100, with at least three different P-wave shapes in one lead, usually in acutely ill patients. She has one normal P-wave shape at 72. Tell: multifocal needs both tachycardia and changing P waves, and she has neither.

Atrial fibrillation is irregularly irregular with absent P waves. She has a normal P wave before every QRS, and her irregularity follows her breathing. Tell: patterned irregularity with P waves is sinus arrhythmia; patternless irregularity without P waves is fibrillation.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following ventricular dysrhythmias: a. Atrioventricular block b. Bundle branch blocks c. Ventricular premature beats d. Ventricular tachycardia e. Ventricular fibrillation f. Torsades de Pointes g. Idioventricular rhythm h. Junctional rhythm i. QT prolongation
set2.q: A 23-year-old competitive cyclist has a regular rhythm at 50 with narrow QRS complexes and no visible P waves on a screening electrocardiogram. He has no symptoms, and his echocardiogram is normal. Which is the most appropriate management?
opts: A permanent pacemaker is for a junctional rhythm caused by complete or high-grade atrioventricular block or by sick sinus syndrome. This cyclist's rhythm comes from high vagal tone in a normal heart and causes no symptoms. Tell: management depends on the cause, and a healthy, asymptomatic athlete needs none.

Atropine is used when a junctional rhythm comes from digitalis toxicity, and as first-line treatment for acute, unstable bradycardia. This cyclist has no symptoms, no drug exposure and a normal heart. Tell: atropine needs a cause like digoxin toxicity or instability, and a healthy athlete has neither.

His training is the likely reason for the rhythm, since increased vagal tone in well-conditioned athletes is a recognized cause of junctional rhythm. Junctional rhythm is generally well tolerated and needs no treatment when asymptomatic in an otherwise healthy person. Tell: an asymptomatic athlete with a normal heart needs no restriction.

Correct. A regular, narrow-complex rhythm at 50 with no visible P waves is a junctional rhythm, usually 40 to 60, and it can be seen in healthy people with increased vagal tone, such as well-conditioned athletes. With no symptoms and a normal echocardiogram in an otherwise healthy cyclist, no treatment is needed.

set2.q: A 31-year-old woman has inappropriate sinus tachycardia at about 110 after a full workup excluded other causes. Her only symptom is awareness of her heartbeat, and she asks whether she needs medication. Which response is most accurate?
opts: She needs a lifelong beta blocker

Beta blockers are not well tolerated in inappropriate sinus tachycardia, which is why it is generally left untreated. Her only symptom is awareness of her heartbeat. Tell: patients tolerate the symptoms better than the treatment, so a lifelong drug is not the usual plan.

Synchronized cardioversion is for hemodynamically unstable tachyarrhythmias such as supraventricular tachycardia, atrial flutter or atrial fibrillation. Inappropriate sinus tachycardia is a sinus rhythm in a stable patient and is generally left untreated. Tell: a sinus rhythm is not shocked; management is removing influencing factors.

Anticoagulation belongs to atrial fibrillation and atrial flutter, guided by stroke risk. Inappropriate sinus tachycardia is a sinus rhythm with a usually benign prognosis, and anticoagulation is not part of its management. Tell: a sinus rhythm, even a fast one, does not bring an anticoagulation decision.

Correct. Inappropriate sinus tachycardia is generally left untreated because patients tolerate the symptoms better than the treatment and the prognosis is usually benign. Management centers on removing influencing factors, such as night-shift work, illicit drugs and medications, rather than on beta blockers, which are poorly tolerated.

set2.q: A 71-year-old man with atrial fibrillation takes warfarin because direct oral anticoagulants are not suitable for him. Which international normalized ratio is the target?
opts: A ratio of 1 to 1.5 falls below the warfarin target for atrial fibrillation, an international normalized ratio (INR) of 2 to 3. Tell: the target range starts at 2, so anything under 2 is not at goal, and direct oral anticoagulants remain the preferred class when suitable.

Correct. If warfarin is used for anticoagulation in atrial fibrillation, as here because direct oral anticoagulants are not suitable, the target international normalized ratio (INR) is 2 to 3. Direct oral anticoagulants are otherwise preferred in nonvalvular atrial fibrillation.

A ratio of 3.5 to 4.5 is above the warfarin target for atrial fibrillation, an international normalized ratio (INR) of 2 to 3. Unstable or high values also add a point to the HAS-BLED (bleeding-risk) score. Tell: the atrial fibrillation target tops out at 3.

A ratio of 4 to 5 is well above the warfarin target for atrial fibrillation, an international normalized ratio (INR) of 2 to 3, and high values count toward bleeding risk on the HAS-BLED (bleeding-risk) score. Tell: remember 2 to 3 for atrial fibrillation on warfarin.

set2.q: A 21-year-old man collapses while playing basketball and arrives with a very fast regular tachycardia. He is alert with a blood pressure of 112/70. A vagal maneuver fails, and adenosine slows the rate to reveal an irregular rhythm with wide QRS complexes, each with a delta wave (slurred upstroke). Which is the next step?
opts: Atropine is first line for acute, symptomatic, unstable bradycardia, a slow rhythm. His problem is a very fast rhythm conducting over an accessory pathway, the opposite of what atropine treats. Tell: atropine answers slow rates; atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White gets procainamide.

Oral beta blockers serve as chronic therapy for focal atrial tachycardia or as a pill-in-the-pocket option for nodal reentry, not as the acute drug here. Atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White revealed by adenosine is treated with intravenous procainamide. Tell: a pre-excited, irregular wide rhythm calls for intravenous procainamide, not an oral rate-control drug.

Correct. Adenosine has slowed the rate and revealed an irregular rhythm with wide complexes and delta waves, which is atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White. In that situation intravenous procainamide is used and adenosine is never repeated; he is alert with a blood pressure of 112/70, so a drug is appropriate.

Adenosine may be repeated in ordinary stable supraventricular tachycardia, but once it reveals atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White it must never be used again. Irregular wide complexes with delta waves are exactly that finding. Tell: delta waves on an irregular rhythm switch the drug to procainamide.

set2.q: A 47-year-old woman has persistent, symptomatic premature atrial contractions despite cutting out caffeine and alcohol. She has no contraindications to beta blockade. Which treatment is first?
opts: Correct. Her premature atrial contractions are persistent and symptomatic even after cutting out caffeine and alcohol, and she has no contraindication to beta blockade. Persistent, symptomatic premature atrial contractions are treated with a beta blocker such as metoprolol if not contraindicated; ablation is kept for frequent beats or those triggering atrial fibrillation.

Intravenous procainamide is used when Wolff-Parkinson-White is known or adenosine reveals atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White. Persistent, symptomatic premature atrial contractions get a beta blocker. Tell: procainamide belongs to pre-excited atrial fibrillation, not to early atrial beats.

Adenosine is used in stable supraventricular tachycardia after a vagal maneuver, to convert the rhythm or slow it enough to reveal P waves. It is not used to suppress premature atrial contractions. Tell: symptomatic early atrial beats that persist after trigger avoidance get metoprolol.

Warfarin is an anticoagulant used in atrial fibrillation, with a target international normalized ratio (INR) of 2 to 3. Premature atrial contractions carry no anticoagulation indication, and persistent symptomatic ones are treated with a beta blocker. Tell: anticoagulants prevent clots; they do not suppress early beats.

set2.q: A 25-year-old man with Wolff-Parkinson-White asks which rhythm would be most dangerous for him. Which answer is most accurate?
opts: Sinus arrhythmia is a normal, physiologic variation in the sinus rate, faster on inspiration and slower on expiration, at 60 to 100. It poses no danger to him. Tell: the danger in Wolff-Parkinson-White is a rate above 200, which atrial fibrillation down the pathway can reach.

Correct. Supraventricular tachycardia usually does not cause syncope or hemodynamic collapse unless the rate goes above 200, and atrial fibrillation associated with an accessory pathway, as in Wolff-Parkinson-White, is one of the rhythms that gets there. In that setting some rates approach 300.

Sinus tachycardia during exercise is a normal physiologic response at over 100 to 160. Collapse from a supraventricular rhythm usually needs a rate above 200, which atrial fibrillation conducting down an accessory pathway can reach. Tell: a sinus rate capped near 160 is not the threat.

Premature atrial contractions are usually benign and asymptomatic, and treatment, if any, is reassurance or a beta blocker. The dangerous rhythm with an accessory pathway is atrial fibrillation, which can drive the rate above 200. Tell: isolated early beats do not cause collapse; a very fast pre-excited fibrillation can.

set2.q: A 26-year-old woman with known Wolff-Parkinson-White has palpitations. Her rhythm is irregularly irregular at rates up to 280 with wide, varying QRS complexes. She is alert with a blood pressure of 110/70. Which treatment must be avoided?
opts: Intravenous procainamide is the drug to use, not avoid, when Wolff-Parkinson-White is known or atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White appears. She is alert with a blood pressure of 110/70, so it suits her now. Tell: in pre-excited atrial fibrillation, procainamide is given and adenosine is the drug to avoid.

Synchronized cardioversion is the treatment for hemodynamically unstable tachyarrhythmias, so it stays available if she becomes unstable. It is not the treatment to avoid. Tell: the one drug that must never be used in atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White is adenosine.

Catheter ablation of the accessory pathway is the first-line chronic treatment for Wolff-Parkinson-White, so planning it for later is appropriate. It is not the treatment to avoid. Tell: ablation is the long-term fix; adenosine is the acute danger.

Correct. An irregularly irregular rhythm up to 280 with wide, varying QRS complexes in known Wolff-Parkinson-White is atrial fibrillation conducting down the accessory pathway. When Wolff-Parkinson-White is known or this rhythm appears, adenosine must never be used; intravenous procainamide is the drug.

set2.q: A 33-year-old woman has abrupt-onset palpitations during a week of little sleep and heavy coffee. Her heart rate is 160 and regular, and every QRS is preceded by an identical P wave whose shape differs from her baseline P wave. She has no heart disease. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Sinus tachycardia keeps a uniform P wave matching the normal sinus shape, and it can follow stimulants such as coffee. Her P wave differs from her baseline shape, which places the source outside the sinus node, and the onset was abrupt. Tell: compare with the baseline P wave; a new, consistent abnormal shape means an ectopic focus.
ruled out by a stated finding

Atrial flutter shows sawtooth waves at an atrial rate of 250 or more that outnumber the QRS complexes. She has one discrete abnormal P wave before each QRS at 160. Tell: one P wave per QRS means an atrial focus; more sawtooth waves than QRS complexes means flutter.

Correct. A regular tachycardia at 160 with one identical P wave before each QRS, shaped differently from her baseline P wave, comes from a single ectopic focus in the atria outside the sinus node: focal atrial tachycardia. It is commonly seen without heart disease when metabolic demand rises, and most people report abrupt-onset palpitations, as she does.

Multifocal atrial tachycardia is irregular, with at least three P-wave shapes in the same lead, and usually arises in acutely ill patients with severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease or heart failure. Her rhythm is regular with one identical abnormal P wave and no heart disease. Tell: one abnormal shape is focal; three or more is multifocal.
ruled out by a stated finding

set2.q: A 30-year-old woman with a stable, regular narrow complex tachycardia at 180 is being treated in the emergency department. She is alert with a normal blood pressure. Which treatment should be avoided at this stage?
opts: A vagal maneuver is the first-line step for stable supraventricular tachycardia, so it is exactly what she should get, not something to avoid. She is alert with a normal blood pressure, which makes it the right opening move. Tell: in a stable narrow tachycardia, the vagal maneuver comes first and adenosine second.

Adenosine is the second step for stable supraventricular tachycardia if a vagal maneuver fails, and it may convert the rhythm or slow it to reveal P waves. It is appropriate here, not to be avoided. Tell: in stable supraventricular tachycardia, the option to avoid is the shock, not the drugs.

Adenosine may be given twice as needed in stable supraventricular tachycardia, so a second dose is appropriate. Tell: a repeat adenosine dose is part of the stable pathway; the treatment to avoid is an unsynchronized shock, which is not the listed shock for this rhythm even when unstable.

Correct. She has a stable, regular narrow complex tachycardia at 180, alert with a normal blood pressure, so she gets a vagal maneuver first, then adenosine, which may be given twice. Even if she became unstable, the shock would be synchronized cardioversion, a timed shock at decreased voltage, so an unsynchronized shock is the treatment to avoid.

set2.q: A 16-year-old boy has a delta wave (a slurred upstroke of the QRS) with a short PR interval on a screening electrocardiogram but no symptoms. His parents ask what the finding means. Which explanation is most accurate?
opts: An extra pathway causing fast rhythms

Correct. A short PR interval with a delta wave on a resting tracing is pre-excitation, consistent with an accessory pathway (bundle of Kent) and the potential for atrioventricular reentrant tachycardia. That is Wolff-Parkinson-White, and for chronic management catheter ablation of the pathway is first line.
A sign of a prior heart attack

A prior heart attack is not what a short PR with a delta wave means. That pair is pre-excitation, the sign of an accessory pathway (bundle of Kent) that can carry reentrant tachycardia. Tell: a delta wave points to an extra pathway, not to damaged muscle.

Well-conditioned athletes can show sinus bradycardia as an adaptive response, not a short PR with a delta wave. That pair is pre-excitation, consistent with an accessory pathway (bundle of Kent), not an effect of training. Tell: an athletic heart may beat slowly; a delta wave means an extra pathway.
A slow node needing a pacemaker

Pre-excitation means the impulse reaches the ventricles early through an extra pathway, which gives the short PR; it is not a slow node. Pacemakers are for symptomatic bradycardia. Tell: a short PR means faster, not slower, conduction to the ventricles.

set2.q: A 26-year-old marathon runner has a resting heart rate of 48 at a preparticipation physical. He denies dizziness, fainting or chest pain. The electrocardiogram shows a regular rhythm with a normal P wave before every narrow QRS and a PR interval of 0.16 seconds. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: A permanent pacemaker is for chronic, symptomatic bradycardia. This runner denies dizziness, fainting and chest pain, and his slow rate is an adaptive response to conditioning. Tell: a pacemaker needs symptoms that track the slow rate, and none are present here.

Sinus bradycardia is seen in healthy people as an adaptive response, particularly in well-conditioned athletes. His training is the reason for the slow rate, and with no symptoms nothing needs treating or stopping. Tell: an athlete's asymptomatic sinus bradycardia gets reassurance only, not activity limits.

Correct. A regular rhythm at 48 with a normal P wave before every narrow QRS and a PR of 0.16 seconds is sinus bradycardia. In a well-conditioned marathon runner with no dizziness, fainting or chest pain it is an adaptive response, and asymptomatic sinus bradycardia is not treated.

Atropine is first line for acute, symptomatic, hemodynamically unstable bradycardia. This runner is well, with no dizziness, fainting or chest pain. Tell: atropine needs symptoms and instability; an asymptomatic athlete with sinus bradycardia needs neither a drug nor a device.

opts: If it lasts over an hour

Duration is not the threshold given for collapse; supraventricular tachycardia usually does not cause syncope or hemodynamic collapse unless the rate goes above 200. Tell: the number to remember is a rate above 200, not minutes or hours.

Correct. Supraventricular tachycardia usually does not lead to syncope or hemodynamic collapse unless the heart rate goes above 200, as can happen with atrioventricular reentry, nodal reentry or atrial fibrillation with an accessory pathway. His episodes at about 170 cause palpitations but not collapse, which fits.

A rate above 100 simply defines a tachycardia, and his episodes at 170 have never made him faint. Collapse from supraventricular tachycardia usually needs a rate above 200. Tell: tachycardia starts at 100; collapse usually needs over 200.

Older age can make symptoms more pronounced, as can structural heart disease, but collapse is tied to the rate going above 200, not to a particular age. Tell: age worsens symptoms; a rate above 200 drives collapse.

set2.q: A 72-year-old woman with symptomatic sinus bradycardia at 45 also has hypertension that needs a new medication. Which antihypertensive should be avoided?
opts: Correct. She already has symptomatic sinus bradycardia at 45, and nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers such as verapamil are listed, with beta blockers and digoxin, as drug causes of sinus bradycardia. Adding verapamil would slow her further, so it should be avoided.

Lisinopril is not among the listed drug causes of sinus bradycardia, which are beta blockers, nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers and digoxin. It is not the antihypertensive to avoid here. Tell: in a patient with sinus bradycardia, avoid the drugs on the slow list.

Chlorthalidone is not among the listed drug causes of sinus bradycardia. The drugs to avoid in symptomatic sinus bradycardia are beta blockers, nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers and digoxin. Tell: only the drug on the slow list needs avoiding, and that is verapamil.

Losartan is not among the listed drug causes of sinus bradycardia. Verapamil, a nondihydropyridine calcium channel blocker, is on that list with beta blockers and digoxin. Tell: the one option here that slows the sinus node is verapamil.

set2.q: A 30-year-old woman with known atrioventricular nodal reentry has a regular narrow complex tachycardia at 178. She is stable. Which treatment almost always terminates it?
opts: Synchronized cardioversion is rarely required in atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia and is held for hemodynamic instability. She is stable, so she gets vagal maneuvers or adenosine first. Tell: a stable patient with nodal reentry almost never needs a shock.

Intravenous procainamide is used when Wolff-Parkinson-White is known or when adenosine reveals atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White. She has known nodal reentry, a circuit within the node with no accessory pathway. Tell: procainamide answers an accessory pathway; nodal reentry answers to vagal maneuvers or adenosine.

Catheter ablation offers a definitive cure, over 95 percent, for a select subset of patients with nodal reentry, but it is a planned procedure, not how an acute episode is stopped. Her stable episode now responds to vagal maneuvers or adenosine. Tell: the question asks what terminates the episode, not what prevents the next one.

Correct. She is stable with a regular narrow tachycardia at 178 and known nodal reentry, and atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia almost always terminates with vagal maneuvers or adenosine. An educated patient whose vagal maneuver works at home usually does not need urgent medical attention.

set2.q: A 74-year-old woman with decompensated heart failure and chronic lung disease develops an irregular tachycardia with three different P-wave shapes in one lead. What does this rhythm signal about her course?
opts: A permanent pacemaker treats chronic symptomatic bradycardia. Multifocal atrial tachycardia is a fast rhythm managed by treating the underlying condition, and it signals a poor prognosis. Tell: the question asks what the rhythm signals, and the answer is how sick she is.

Correct. An irregular tachycardia with three P-wave shapes in one lead is multifocal atrial tachycardia, and in decompensated heart failure with lung disease it reflects acute illness with right heart stress or pulmonary hypertension. Multifocal atrial tachycardia is a poor prognostic sign, and management is treating the underlying condition.

Benign describes focal atrial tachycardia, which is commonly seen without heart disease. Multifocal atrial tachycardia occurs when patients with severe lung disease or heart failure are acutely ill and is a poor prognostic sign. Tell: focal is generally benign; multifocal marks serious illness.

Multifocal atrial tachycardia appears when patients with severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease or heart failure are acutely ill, with right heart stress. It is a poor prognostic sign, not a marker of recovery. Tell: this rhythm tracks how sick the patient is.
