set2.q: A 36-year-old man has a regular tachycardia at 170 with an identical, abnormally shaped P wave before every QRS. Adenosine briefly slows the ventricular response, but the abnormal atrial rhythm continues unchanged afterward. Which rhythm does this response point to?
opts: Multifocal atrial tachycardia is irregular, with at least three different P-wave shapes in one lead from multiple foci. This rhythm is regular with one identical abnormal P wave before every QRS, which takes a single focus. Tell: one abnormal P shape is focal; three or more shapes is multifocal.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. A regular tachycardia at 170 with one identical abnormal P wave before every QRS comes from a single ectopic atrial focus. Adenosine is a diagnostic tool here because it is usually less effective at terminating focal atrial tachycardia than the node-dependent reentry rhythms, so brief slowing with the atrial rhythm carrying on fits.

Nodal reentrant tachycardia is a circuit within the atrioventricular node and almost always terminates with vagal maneuvers or adenosine; its P waves are hidden. Here a visible abnormal P wave precedes every QRS and the atrial rhythm survives adenosine. Tell: termination with adenosine suggests nodal reentry; persistence suggests focal atrial tachycardia.
ruled out by a stated finding

Orthodromic atrioventricular reentrant tachycardia runs through the atrioventricular node, and adenosine is first line for it; its P waves are hidden or retrograde, after the QRS. This rhythm shows an abnormal P wave before each QRS that persists after adenosine. Tell: a rhythm that keeps going despite nodal block is atrial, not node-dependent reentry.
ruled out by a stated finding

set2.q: A 70-year-old man with sick sinus syndrome has pauses on monitoring that alternate with runs of ventricular tachycardia. Which device is indicated?
opts: Observation is appropriate in sick sinus syndrome only when symptoms do not correlate with episodes of bradycardia. Tachy-brady syndrome with ventricular tachycardia needs a permanent pacemaker with an automatic implantable cardioverter-defibrillator. Tell: ventricular tachycardia as the fast phase means adding a defibrillator.

Ablation alone is not the listed device answer for tachy-brady syndrome. The pauses need a permanent pacemaker, and because the tachyarrhythmia is ventricular tachycardia, the pacemaker comes with an automatic implantable cardioverter-defibrillator. Tell: pauses need pacing; ventricular tachycardia adds a defibrillator.

Correct. Pauses alternating with runs of a tachyarrhythmia are tachy-brady syndrome, which often needs a permanent pacemaker. When the tachyarrhythmia is ventricular tachycardia, as here, the patient needs a permanent pacemaker with an automatic implantable cardioverter-defibrillator.

A permanent pacemaker alone covers the pauses of tachy-brady syndrome, but when the tachyarrhythmia is ventricular tachycardia the listed device is a pacemaker with an automatic implantable cardioverter-defibrillator. Tell: ventricular tachycardia is the trigger to add the defibrillator.

set2.q: A 69-year-old woman with severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is admitted in an acute exacerbation. She is tachycardic and irregular, and her electrocardiogram shows three or more different P-wave shapes in one lead with a P wave before each QRS. Which is the most important treatment for this rhythm?
opts: Correct. An irregular tachycardia with three or more P-wave shapes and a P wave before each QRS is multifocal atrial tachycardia, and in an acute chronic obstructive pulmonary disease exacerbation it reflects right heart stress from acute illness. Management is treating the underlying condition; a beta blocker or nondihydropyridine calcium channel blocker may be added in hospital.

Synchronized cardioversion is used for hemodynamically unstable tachycardias, such as unstable focal atrial tachycardia. Multifocal atrial tachycardia is managed by treating the underlying condition, here her chronic obstructive pulmonary disease exacerbation. Tell: multifocal atrial tachycardia is a marker of acute illness and a poor prognostic sign, so treat the cause.

Catheter ablation is usually curative, about 90 percent, for focal atrial tachycardia, which has a single ectopic focus to target. Her rhythm comes from multiple foci provoked by an acute exacerbation, so the fix is treating the lung disease. Tell: one focus can be ablated; multiple foci from acute illness are treated at the cause.

Adenosine terminates node-dependent reentry and is usually less effective even for focal atrial tachycardia, where it serves mainly as a diagnostic tool. Her irregular rhythm with several P-wave shapes is driven by acute lung disease, which adenosine does not touch. Tell: in multifocal atrial tachycardia the target is the lung disease, not the node.

set2.q: A 72-year-old woman has sinus pauses of up to 2 seconds at night on an ambulatory monitor. Her occasional dizziness happens only when she stands up quickly and never during the pauses. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Catheter ablation is used for tachycardias, such as focal atrial tachycardia or an accessory pathway. Her finding is brief night-time sinus pauses that do not match her symptoms. Tell: ablation removes fast circuits; uncorrelated pauses call for observation.

Correct. In sick sinus syndrome the key step is to confirm whether symptoms correlate with episodes of bradycardia. Her night-time pauses cause no symptoms, and her dizziness occurs only on standing quickly, never during the pauses, so with no correlation observation is appropriate.

A permanent pacemaker is placed in sick sinus syndrome when symptomatic bradycardia is confirmed, meaning symptoms correlate with the slow episodes. Her dizziness comes on standing, never during the pauses. Tell: no correlation, no pacemaker; observe instead.

Atropine is first line for acute, symptomatic, hemodynamically unstable bradycardia. She is stable, and her pauses cause no symptoms. Tell: atropine needs an unstable patient; uncorrelated night-time pauses need observation.

set2.q: A 58-year-old woman has a slow sinus rhythm at 38 six hours after an inferior myocardial infarction. She feels faint and her blood pressure is 80/50. Each narrow QRS has a normal P wave before it. Which drug should be given first?
opts: Diltiazem is a nondihydropyridine calcium channel blocker, a class listed with beta blockers and digoxin as a drug cause of sinus bradycardia. Giving it at a rate of 38 with a blood pressure of 80/50 would deepen the problem. Tell: drugs that cause bradycardia never rescue it; atropine does.

Adenosine is used in stable supraventricular tachycardia after a vagal maneuver, to convert the rhythm or slow it enough to reveal P waves. Slowing a sinus rhythm already at 38 is the opposite of what she needs. Tell: adenosine is for a fast narrow rhythm; unstable sinus bradycardia gets atropine.

Correct. A sinus rhythm at 38 with a normal P wave before each narrow QRS, faintness and a blood pressure of 80/50 is acute, symptomatic, hemodynamically unstable sinus bradycardia; sinus node ischemia is a listed cause, fitting the infarction. Atropine is first line, followed by a temporary pacemaker if it fails.

Metoprolol is a beta blocker, and beta blockers are a listed cause of sinus bradycardia, so it would slow her further at a rate of 38. Beta blockers are used for fast rhythms, such as rate control in stable atrial flutter. Tell: a hypotensive, faint patient with a slow sinus rate needs atropine, not a rate-slowing drug.

set2.q: A 65-year-old woman has new atrial fibrillation at 146 with palpitations. She is alert, her blood pressure is 132/84, and she has no chest pain or breathlessness. Which is the most appropriate initial treatment?
opts: Mapping and ablation is a later option in atrial fibrillation management, not the first treatment of a new rapid ventricular response. Her immediate need is to slow the rate with intravenous rate control. Tell: new, fast and stable atrial fibrillation starts with intravenous rate control.

Atropine is first line for acute, symptomatic, unstable bradycardia, a slow rhythm. Her atrial fibrillation is already fast at 146, so raising the rate is the opposite of the goal. Tell: atropine is for slow and unstable; a stable rapid ventricular response needs intravenous rate control.

Correct. New atrial fibrillation at 146 is rapid ventricular response, and with a blood pressure of 132/84, a clear mind and no chest pain or breathlessness she is hemodynamically stable. Stable atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response is treated with intravenous rate control, with anticoagulation planned for all.

Synchronized cardioversion is for hemodynamically unstable atrial fibrillation, such as with severe heart failure, hypotension or an acute myocardial infarction. She is alert with a blood pressure of 132/84 and no chest pain or breathlessness. Tell: a fast rate alone is not instability; check blood pressure and symptoms.

set2.q: A 68-year-old man with coronary artery disease has frequent premature atrial contractions (early beats with abnormal P waves) on a monitor. Which sustained rhythm may these beats go on to precede in him?
opts: Multifocal atrial tachycardia arises in acutely ill patients with severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease or heart failure, not as the sequel of premature atrial contractions. In heart disease these beats may precede supraventricular tachycardia, atrial fibrillation or atrial flutter. Tell: the listed sequels are fibrillation, flutter and supraventricular tachycardia.

Complete heart block is not among the rhythms premature atrial contractions are listed as preceding. In a patient with heart disease they may lead into paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia, atrial fibrillation or atrial flutter. Tell: premature atrial beats lead into fast atrial rhythms, not into block.

Correct. In patients with heart disease, such as his coronary artery disease, premature atrial contractions may precede paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia, atrial fibrillation or atrial flutter. Because his are frequent, the next step is also to look for underlying structural heart disease.

Ventricular fibrillation is not among the rhythms premature atrial contractions are listed as preceding; these beats begin in the atria and lead into atrial rhythms. In heart disease they may precede supraventricular tachycardia, atrial fibrillation or atrial flutter. Tell: an atrial trigger leads into an atrial rhythm.

set2.q: A 37-year-old woman has infrequent, well-tolerated episodes of atrioventricular nodal reentry that sometimes outlast her vagal maneuver. She does not want daily medication or a procedure. Which option fits her best?
opts: Adenosine is used in the acute setting, after a vagal maneuver, to terminate nodal reentry; it is not the listed home option. The home option for nodal reentry is a pill-in-the-pocket beta blocker or nondihydropyridine calcium channel blocker. Tell: pill in pocket means a beta blocker or calcium channel blocker, not adenosine.

Anticoagulation is part of managing atrial fibrillation and atrial flutter. Nodal reentry is a regular reentry circuit within the node and is not managed with anticoagulation. Tell: her options are vagal maneuvers, a pill in the pocket or ablation.

Correct. Her nodal reentry episodes are infrequent and well tolerated, and she wants neither daily medication nor a procedure. A pill-in-the-pocket beta blocker or nondihydropyridine calcium channel blocker, taken only when an episode starts, is an option for nodal reentry that fits those wishes.

Daily amiodarone is the kind of long-term medication she wants to avoid, and it is not a listed option for nodal reentry; amiodarone appears instead as a chemical cardioversion option for focal atrial tachycardia. The listed option that avoids daily drugs is a pill in the pocket. Tell: occasional episodes, occasional pill.

set2.q: A 66-year-old man with stable atrial fibrillation at 92 asks why the plan is to control his heart rate rather than shock him back into normal rhythm today. Which explanation is most accurate?
opts: Synchronized cardioversion is used in atrial fibrillation, immediately for instability and electively as an outpatient after 21 days of anticoagulation. The reason it is not done today is that he is stable and has not yet had 21 days of anticoagulation. Tell: shocks work; timing is the issue.

Sinus rhythm can be restored later, by outpatient cardioversion after 21 days of anticoagulation or by mapping and ablation. Today the plan is rate control because he is stable. Tell: the delay is about anticoagulation first, not about the rhythm being permanent.

Rate control slows the heart; it does not address clots. Anticoagulation, guided by the stroke-risk score, is what addresses stroke risk, and 21 days of it must precede an elective cardioversion. Tell: rate control treats the rate; anticoagulation handles the clot risk.

Correct. He is stable at 92, without rapid ventricular response, so management is rate control, with anticoagulation planned for all patients with atrial fibrillation. An elective outpatient cardioversion comes only after 21 days of anticoagulation, which is why he is not shocked today.

set2.q: A 34-year-old man has occasional premature junctional contractions (early narrow beats with no visible P wave) on a monitor and is anxious about them. He has no symptoms and no heart disease. Which approach is most appropriate?
opts: A beta blocker such as metoprolol is used for premature junctional contractions only when they are frequent, over 10 per minute or multifocal, or when symptoms persist. His are occasional and he has no symptoms, so lifelong treatment is not indicated. Tell: no symptoms plus infrequent beats means reassurance.

Catheter ablation is not among the options for premature junctional contractions; even frequent or persistently symptomatic ones are handled with a search for structural heart disease and a beta blocker. His beats are occasional and cause no symptoms. Tell: infrequent, asymptomatic junctional beats need reassurance only.

A permanent pacemaker is for slow rhythms, such as a junctional rhythm caused by complete or high-grade atrioventricular block or by sick sinus syndrome. He has occasional early beats on an otherwise normal rhythm, not a slow escape rhythm. Tell: a pacemaker treats bradycardia, not premature beats.

Correct. His premature junctional contractions are occasional, he has no symptoms and no heart disease, and no treatment is needed for asymptomatic, infrequent beats. Reassurance about the benign nature of the rhythm is often enough to ease an anxious patient like him.
